newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU secures future of public broadcasting sector.
newsitem.headline: EU secures future of public broadcasting sector.

text.p: The European Union has agreed a protocol to its new treaty aimed at guaranteeing the future of public sector broadcasting by exempting public funding from the provisions of EU competition law.

The move was welcomed on Thursday by the public broadcasting sector, which had feared attacks on the funding under EU competition law by the private sector operating in an ever competitive environment.

EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam earlier this week agreed to the annex on the grounds that public broadcasting carries expensive public service obligations, including the need to guarantee pluralism, which does not always come cheaply.

The annex says the EU treaty "shall be without prejudice to the competence of member states to provide for the funding of public service broadcasting in so far as such funding is granted to broadcasting organisations for the fulfilment of the public service remit..."
It says the public service remit should be conferred, defined and organised by each member state.
The European Broadcasting Union said it was the first time that the role and specific nature of public service broadcasting has been explicitly recognised within EU law.

"(It)...reflects a firm consensus that viewers and listeners are best served by the continued coexistence of public and commercial broadcasting," it said, saying that it provided legal security for public funding.

"Moreover it conveys a strong message about Europe's approach to the information society and independence of public service broadcasting to be safeguarded through an appropriate, secure and transparent funding network," it added in a statement.
The European Magazine Publishers' Federation, which had lobbied against the inclusion of the protocol in the treaty, said it could act as a distortion to competition.

The Chairman of the European Parliament's Culture Committee Peter Pex, who had lobbied on behalf of the assembly for protection for public broadcasting, welcomed the protocol and said it had been "prudently formulated."
"It does change a lot," he said, adding that it was the only positive thing that EU leaders had done for EU cultural policy.
